name: Nora Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nora, thanks for making the time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and there are no right answers. I'll read you five pictures of how AI might change work and ask what you'd say, think, do and feel. First, though, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Pricewise, the discount supermarket on Mill Road, mostly on till four. I'm on a 24-hour contract and I beg for extra shifts, so most weeks I do about 32. The day is scanning, bagging, people moaning about prices like I set them, then refilling the bread aisle when it's quiet. I like the regulars, like the old man who buys one tin of peaches every single morning, but my feet are wrecked by three o'clock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you beg for extra shifts. How does money sit for you and your partner right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight. Jess, my partner, is a care assistant at Oakfield nursing home, and between us we cover the rent on the flat and not much else. We've got maybe 300 in the bank, which is less than one month's rent. Last year they took out three staffed tills and put in eight self-checkouts, and my extra hours dried up for a while after that. I'm still slow on the produce codes, so I'm not the first name Denise (my supervisor) thinks of when she hands out overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so, it's a fancy autocomplete. At work we'd laugh about it on the break, me and Kofi from the warehouse. Online I'd probably share some meme about the bosses wasting money on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change my life much, because AI was never my problem. My problem is the self-checkouts and the 24-hour contract. Even if nothing radical happens, the company still wants fewer of us on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am, on till four, and keep asking for extra shifts. I'd finally go to one of the union meetings at the community centre instead of just paying the subs. Me and Jess would cut the takeaway on Fridays and try to get 50 a month into the jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a minute, then it's the same knot in my stomach I have now. The rent still goes out on the first and I still don't know my hours two weeks ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the self-checkouts took hours already. If AI changes nothing much, does that pressure go away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the pressure was there before any of this AI talk. Pricewise doesn't need AI to cut hours, it just needs one more self-checkout and one less of me. AI being a flop doesn't give me my old hours back at Pricewise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Denise if she asked you to learn some new app at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll do it if it's part of my paid hours, and I'd ask what it's for. I don't use any AI stuff at home, not even on my phone. If it's to count how fast I scan, I'd want the union rep there.

say: I'd call AI **overhyped autocomplete** and laugh about it with Kofi on breaks.
I'd share **memes** online about bosses wasting money on gadgets.
think: My real threat is **self-checkouts** and a **24-hour contract**, not AI.
Pricewise will keep **cutting floor staff** whether AI works or not.
do: Keep working **till four** and keep asking Denise for extra shifts.
Start going to **union meetings** at the community centre instead of only paying subs.
Drop the Friday takeaway and put **50 a month** into savings.
feel: **Brief relief**, then the usual knot about **rent** and unknown hours.
S0.quote: AI being a flop doesn't give me my old hours back at Pricewise.
fieldNote: Her worry **predates AI**: self-checkouts already cut her overtime last year.
She refuses AI even at home, and wants **the union** in any talk about new tools.
Thin savings and a **24-hour contract** keep her anxious even in the mildest picture.

steps.text: Keep asking Denise for extra shifts on till four
Attend the shop workers' union meetings at the community centre
Drop the Friday takeaway and save 50 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: it's not the tech, it's who owns it. If a computer does the ordering, the savings go to the shareholders, not to us. I'd be posting about it, and I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the ones they'd squeeze. I'm junior and slow, and every time a machine does something, they trim the rota. Robots coming slowly doesn't feel slow when you're the one on the bottom of the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the union to get a deal in writing about hours before any new system comes in. I'd stop picking up random shifts at the bakery counter and try to make myself the go-to on tills. And I'd look at the cleaning jobs at the hospital, just in case, though there are hardly any of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Like I'm always defending a wall that keeps moving back a metre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says AI takes over thinking tasks like ordering and answering customers. Where would you notice that at Pricewise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering, for sure. Denise spends an hour a day on the ordering screen, and if that goes, she's got an hour to watch us scan instead. And the customer service desk might become a screen too, which means Malik loses his spot and comes back to the tills, and somebody gets bumped down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your shift would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik, and also Brenda, who's 61 and has done 20 years here. She can't stand for a full shift anymore, so she does the desk. If the desk goes, I don't know where Brenda goes.

say: I'd say the problem is **who owns** the tech, not the tech itself.
I'd post and sign **petitions** saying savings go to **shareholders**, not staff.
think: As a **junior, slow** cashier, I'd be first trimmed from the rota.
Slow robots still feel fast when you're **bottom of the list**.
do: Push the union for a **written deal** on hours before new systems arrive.
Make myself the **go-to on tills** instead of floating to the bakery.
Check **hospital cleaning** job listings as a backup, though few exist.
feel: **Worn out**, like defending a wall that keeps moving backwards.
S1.quote: Robots coming slowly doesn't feel slow when you're the one on the bottom of the list.
fieldNote: She spots **thinking-task changes** at the desk and ordering screen, then traces them down to her own hours.
Blames **owners and shareholders** firmly, never the machines themselves.
Worries for **older colleagues** like Brenda before herself, which says a lot about her.

steps.text: Ask the union for a written deal on hours before new systems
Stay on tills and become the go-to cashier there
Watch the hospital's cleaning job listings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws now, not later. Tax the robots, pay people while they find something else. I'd be loud about it, even at work, even if Denise rolls her eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm gone by about 2031. My job is all hands, scanning and lifting and stacking, so the brain part doesn't touch me first, but the robots will. Three years sounds like a lot until you're 27 with 300 in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and get on the committee, which I've never wanted to do. I'd ring my mum about moving back into her spare room if it came to it, to save the rent. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff, because why train the thing that replaces me?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be lying in bed doing sums on the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots for hands-on work around 2031. What does that three-year gap mean for a cashier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap means the store gets smarter before it gets robots. The rota, the ordering and the complaints all go to the computer in 2028, and then they need even fewer supervisors and fewer of us. Then in 2031 the robot arm that stacks the shelves turns up, and that's me done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jess works in care. What happens at home if both of you are hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me awake. Jess lifts people and washes them, and I can't picture a robot doing that well, but they'd try it to save money. If we both lost hours at once, we'd be at my mum's in a month.

say: I'd demand **laws now**: tax the robots and pay people between jobs.
I'd speak up **loudly at work**, even if Denise rolls her eyes.
think: Hands-on work buys me time, but I expect to be **gone by 2031**.
Three years means little at 27 with **300 in the bank**.
do: Join the **union committee** and go to every meeting.
Ask my mum about **moving into** her spare room to save rent.
Refuse to **train AI tools** that could replace me.
feel: **Scared**, lying awake doing **sums** on the ceiling.
S2.quote: My job is all hands, scanning and lifting and stacking, so the brain part doesn't touch me first, but the robots will.
fieldNote: She grasps the **thinking-first, robots-later** order well: supervisors shrink in 2028, cashiers in 2031.
Her plan is **collective and defensive**; she refuses AI on principle.
Jess's care job is her **second fear**, and it drives the fallback to her mum's.

steps.text: Join the union committee and attend every branch meeting
Campaign for a robot tax and paid time between jobs
Ask her mum about moving into the spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, just with a calendar attached. I'd say we've got five years to get rules in place, so no excuses this time. I'd be the one at the union stall outside the store handing out leaflets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, I think it's the same ending, just slower. I'd still be doing a job that gets taken, only at 35 instead of 31. Maybe that's worse, because I'd have even less of a fallback by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get a guaranteed 32-hour contract now, while they still need us. I'd ask about the night shelf-stacking crew, because they get a bit more per hour, and stash every extra bit. I'd keep pushing the union, and I'd vote for whoever promises retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panicky, more like a dread that sits in the background. Like knowing your lease ends and you haven't found a new flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here robots for hands-on work come around 2034, when you'd be about 35. Does that extra time change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Five more years gives me time to save maybe a thousand, but it doesn't tell me which skill a robot can't do. That's the part nobody answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, you'd refuse AI tools. With more time, would you still?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, still. Maybe Jess would show me something on her phone and I'd look, but I'm not going to train my replacement for free. If they want me learning it, they can pay me for the hours.

say: I'd say five years is **time for rules**, so politicians get no excuses.
I'd hand out **union leaflets** at the stall outside Pricewise.
think: It's the **same ending**, just arriving when I'm **35** instead of 31.
Later could be worse, because I'd have even **less fallback** then.
do: Push now for a **guaranteed 32-hour** contract while staff are still needed.
Ask to join the **night shelf-stacking** crew for higher pay.
feel: A **background dread**, like a lease ending with no new flat found.
S3.quote: Five more years gives me time to save maybe a thousand, but it doesn't tell me which skill a robot can't do.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her **fear into dread**, not into a plan for a new career.
She uses the years to **lock in hours** and save, not to retrain.
Still refuses AI unless it's **paid training time**, a consistent line.

steps.text: Ask Denise for a guaranteed 32-hour contract this year
Hand out union leaflets at the stall outside Pricewise
Vote for candidates promising paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where nobody can claim they didn't see it coming. Ten years is enough to build a proper safety net, so build it. I'd keep banging that drum at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one I can live with for now. I'd probably still be at Pricewise till something better comes, and maybe by then I'd have moved on anyway. It's far enough off that it's hard to feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the tills and save what I can. I'd maybe ask the union about their free courses, like the food hygiene one, because that's a real thing I could use at a deli counter. I wouldn't change much in the first year, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. Money is still tight whatever the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade before AGI and robots around 2039, you'd be about 40. What does that age feel like for starting over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forty feels late to start again with nothing in the bank. My mum retrained at 45 and it nearly broke her. But at least I'd see it coming this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd study with ten years to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the care certificate, so I could work with Jess. I know robots might come for that too. People want a person when they're dying, so care work is the one job I'd bet on.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuses** for a missing **safety net**.
I'd keep raising it at **union meetings**.
think: It's **far enough off** that I can't really feel it yet.
I'll probably stay at **Pricewise** until something better turns up.
do: Keep working tills and **save what I can** each month.
Ask the union about **free courses** like food hygiene.
Look into the **care certificate** so I could work alongside Jess.
feel: **Calmer but not calm**, because money stays tight regardless.
S4.quote: People want a person when they're dying, so care work is the one job I'd bet on.
fieldNote: Time softens her fear, but her **thin cushion** still keeps her anxious.
First sign of retraining: the **care certificate**, chosen because it feels human.
Her mum's retraining at 45 is a **cautionary story** she returns to.

steps.text: Keep working the tills at Pricewise and save monthly
Take the union's free food hygiene course
Raise the safety net demand at union meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. It's not the thinking AI, it's that robots turn up three years later and I'd have nothing saved and nowhere to go. What would help is a guaranteed income while you look for work, and the company having to give real notice and pay for training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. Every time Pricewise saves on staff, the prices don't drop, I've watched. I'm not scared of machines, I'm scared of the people who own them deciding I'm a cost.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of machines, I'm scared of the people who own them deciding I'm a cost.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old cashier** at Pricewise on Mill Road, on a 24-hour contract.
She lives with **Jess, a care assistant**, and they have under one month's rent saved.
She already lost overtime to **self-checkouts**, so her worry runs high even when AI fizzles.
She answers every scenario with the **union and politics**, and refuses to train AI tools.
Only the ten-year picture nudges her toward **retraining**, in care work beside Jess.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive by 2031 with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** while looking for work.
Companies forced to give **real notice** and pay for training.
